title.v: Cosmos SDK Appchain Development Services

c.v: Design, build and launch an application-specific blockchain that you control.
Your protocol has outgrown shared block space. You need control of transaction ordering, fees, validator economics and upgrades, which a smart contract on someone else's chain cannot give you.
ClickMasters provides Cosmos SDK appchain development

from the first architecture decision to a running mainnet. We design the custom modules, consensus parameters, token economics, IBC connections and validator infrastructure, and we support the chain after launch.

We build on the current, supported Cosmos stack: the Cosmos SDK, CometBFT consensus, IBC (including IBC v2 connections to Ethereum), and CosmWasm or Cosmos EVM where you need smart contracts. We also tell you plainly when an appchain is the wrong choice.

title.v: Do You Need a Cosmos Appchain? A Decision Framework

c.v: An appchain is a long-term commitment. You are launching a network that needs validators, a security budget, infrastructure and governance for as long as it runs. Before any code is written, we work through this decision with you. Sometimes the right answer is to stay on an existing chain.

blocks.alt: Decision tree comparing smart contracts, rollups and Cosmos appchains

c.v: Signals an appchain is the right architecture
You need control over block production.

Order books, auctions and liquidation engines often need custom transaction ordering, matching logic or MEV protections, which are hard to get on a general-purpose chain. With ABCI 2.0, a Cosmos appchain decides how its blocks are proposed and validated.
Your fees should follow your product, not someone else's gas market.
Charge fees in your own token or a stablecoin, sponsor fees for new users, and keep costs predictable when another application on a shared chain goes viral.
Data must be part of consensus.

Validators can attach data, such as oracle prices, to their votes (vote extensions). The chain then agrees on that data every block, secured by your own validator set rather than a separate oracle network. Validators still source the data from off-chain feeds.
You need protocol-level features a contract cannot implement.
Examples are native compliance checks before transactions execute, custom account types, built-in staking rewards, or logic that runs automatically every block.
Governance and upgrades must be yours.
Your community or consortium decides when and how the protocol changes, not the governance of a host chain.
You need permissioning.
Regulated or consortium networks can restrict who validates, who deploys contracts and who transacts.
Signals you should not build one (yet)
Your product has not found users.
A smart contract on an existing network launches faster and inherits wallets, liquidity and security on day one. Many successful appchains started as contracts.
Composability with one ecosystem is the main value.
If your product depends on synchronous calls to protocols on Ethereum or Solana, a separate chain adds latency and bridging complexity.
You cannot fund a security budget.
A proof-of-stake chain is only as secure as the value staked on it. Validators expect rewards, and a token with little market value buys little security.
No one will own operations.
Someone must coordinate upgrades, watch validator health, maintain relayers and answer incidents, permanently.
Not sure which side you're on? Our
blockchain consulting
team runs a structured feasibility assessment before you commit budget.

title.v: Cosmos SDK, CometBFT, IBC and the Cosmos Hub: How an Appchain Fits Together

c.v: These four names are often confused. The split shows what you build, what you configure, and what comes ready-made. For a broader primer, read our
Cosmos SDK technology overview

blocks.alt: ABCI 2.0 block flow between CometBFT and a Cosmos SDK application

c.v: The application layer: Cosmos SDK.
The Cosmos SDK is an open-source Go framework for the chain's
application
, the state machine that decides what each transaction does. A chain is a set of
modules

. Each module owns part of the state and exposes the messages that can change it. Accounts, balances, staking and governance come ready-made; your product logic lives in custom modules beside them. Everything compiles into one node binary that validators run.
The consensus layer: CometBFT.
CometBFT, the maintained fork of Tendermint Core, gets validators to agree on transaction order and produce blocks.
Safety:
the chain stays safe while validators controlling
less than one-third of voting power
are faulty.
Finality:
a block is final once more than two-thirds of voting power commits it. There are no reorganisations to wait out.
The application and CometBFT communicate through
ABCI 2.0
, which gives your application a say in block construction:
PrepareProposal:
the proposer builds a block.
ProcessProposal:
other validators check it.
ExtendVote / VerifyVoteExtension:
validators attach data to their votes.
FinalizeBlock:
the block executes.
The interoperability layer: IBC.

The Inter-Blockchain Communication protocol moves tokens and arbitrary data between chains. Each chain verifies the other's consensus with an on-chain light client. IBC is now a Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust project, and its Go implementation, ibc-go, is a module you add to your chain.
Where the Cosmos Hub fits.
The Cosmos Hub is
one
chain built with the SDK, with ATOM as its token. Building with the SDK does
not
require connecting to the Hub, paying it, or being secured by it. Your appchain is independent and can open IBC connections to the Hub or any other IBC-enabled chain.

rows.v: Go framework for the chain's application logic
Which modules to use and which to build
Validator set size, block timing, mempool strategy
Which chains to connect, which IBC applications to enable
Optional smart contract environments, added as modules
Whether third parties deploy contracts, and in which language

title.v: Custom Cosmos Blockchain Development: SDK Modules for Your Business Logic

c.v: Custom modules are where your appchain becomes your product. A module is native protocol code. It runs on every node, can execute at the start or end of every block, and has direct, permissioned access to other modules. That is more powerful than a smart contract, so it needs more care.

blocks.alt: Anatomy of a custom Cosmos SDK module with keeper, message server and store

c.v: What belongs in a custom module
Native modules suit logic that is
core to the protocol, performance-critical, or needs privileged access
Matching and settlement engines:
order books, auctions and AMMs that run in every block.
Asset issuance and compliance:
tokens with transfer restrictions, allow-lists, freezing or reporting hooks for regulated assets.
Protocol economics:
custom reward distribution, fee routing, buy-back or burn logic.
Automation:
epoch-based processes, interest accrual, expiries and liquidations that must run even when nobody sends a transaction.
Consensus data:
aggregating oracle prices from validator vote extensions.
Logic that changes often, comes from third parties, or does not need privileged access usually belongs in smart contracts instead.
Standard modules we configure, not rewrite

rows.v: Validator set, penalties, rewards, misbehaviour evidence
Validator limits, unbonding period, slashing fractions, commission rules
Inflation model or a custom mint function
Epoch schedules, block and evidence limits

c.v: On permissioned networks we also assess the Cosmos Labs
Enterprise modules

for proof of authority and group governance. They are published under a source-available licence that requires a commercial licence for production use, so we raise the licensing question during architecture, not after launch.
How we engineer modules
Specification first.
Each module starts with a written spec covering state layout, messages, queries, events, invariants and failure cases. You review it before implementation begins.
Protobuf-defined APIs.
One definition generates typed gRPC, REST and CLI interfaces for wallets, frontends and other chains.
Least-privilege keepers.
Modules interact only through narrow keeper interfaces. That limits what a bug in one module can do to another's state.
Deterministic code.
No floating-point arithmetic, unordered map iteration, wall-clock time or external I/O in state transitions. Any of these can halt a chain when nodes disagree.
Ante handler customisation.
Fee logic, transaction filtering and gas rules run before each message executes.
Gas accounting.
Expensive operations are metered so no transaction can consume unbounded resources.
Upgrade-ready state.
Versioned store layouts and migration functions, so later upgrades never need a restart from scratch.

title.v: CometBFT Consensus and Block Production Design

c.v: Consensus is configured, not coded. The configuration still decides how fast, how decentralised and how resilient your chain will be.
Block timing.

Block times come from CometBFT's propose, prevote, precommit and commit timeouts, together with network latency. We tune them for your workload and your validators' geography, and we measure the result on testnet. We don't promise a number before your validators exist.
Validator-set size.
More validators means more decentralisation and censorship resistance, but more voting messages and slower rounds. A public DeFi chain is set up differently from a 10-node consortium network.
Block and transaction limits.
Maximum block size and gas per block shape throughput and protect nodes from oversized blocks.
Application-driven block building.
With PrepareProposal and ProcessProposal your chain can do three things:
enforce ordering rules
include protocol-generated transactions
reject blocks that break application rules
Trading protocols use this for fair ordering and MEV mitigation.
Vote extensions.
Validators sign extra data, such as price observations, in each round, and the application aggregates it in the next block.
Mempool strategy.
Current releases support an application-side mempool, so your chain can prioritise or filter transactions by its own rules.
Performance features.
Recent SDK releases add opt-in parallel execution (Block-STM) and unordered transactions for high-volume senders. We enable them only after benchmarking your workload.
To compare BFT consensus with other designs, see
how consensus mechanisms compare

title.v: Choosing a Security Model: Sovereign PoS, Proof of Authority or Shared Security

c.v: Who secures your chain is the most important economic decision you will make. These are the options as they stand today:
Sovereign proof of stake

rows.v: Your own validators stake your token; misbehaviour is slashed
Public networks with a token that has real value and community
You bootstrap validators and fund their incentives; security scales with token value

c.v: Proof of authority (permissioned)

rows.v: Trust rests on participants' identities and agreements; Enterprise PoA module needs a commercial licence

c.v: External security services

rows.v: Economic security borrowed from another network (for example Bitcoin-staking protocols built on Cosmos)
Teams wanting extra security without a large validator set
Newer designs; extra integration and dependency risk; evaluated case by case

c.v: Interchain Security is no longer an option on the Cosmos Hub.

In 2026 the Hub stopped accepting new consumer chains and removed its provider module, after the remaining consumer chains moved to their own security models. Some vendor pages still advertise "replicated security" or "consumer chains". Treat those as out of date.
For most public appchains the realistic choice is sovereign proof of stake. That is why the validator strategy and the token model must be designed together.

title.v: IBC Integration Services: Connecting Your Appchain

c.v: IBC is the main reason teams choose Cosmos over a standalone chain. Done well, it gives your chain access to assets, users and services on other networks without a custodial bridge. Done carelessly, it brings new failure modes, such as expired clients, stuck packets and unlimited inflows during an exploit. Our IBC integration services cover both sides.
How IBC works, in brief

blocks.alt: How IBC works: light clients, connections, channels and packets relayed between two chains

c.v: Light clients
on each chain track the other chain's validator set and verify its block headers.
Connections
pair two light clients through a handshake.
Channels
link applications over a connection. They are either ordered or unordered.
Packets
carry data with a proof of commitment. The receiving chain writes an
acknowledgement
. If a packet isn't received in time, a
timeout
lets the sender refund or revert.
Relayers
carry packets and proofs between chains. They are trusted only for liveness: a relayer can delay a packet but cannot forge one.
Interchain Accounts (ICA)
Interchain Accounts let your chain
open and control an account on another chain

over IBC. Your appchain can stake, provide liquidity or vote on another network without users bridging assets by hand. Liquid-staking protocols, treasury managers and cross-chain vaults rely on this. We build the controller logic and the acknowledgement handling, so your chain knows when a remote action failed and reacts correctly.
Interchain Queries (ICQ)
Interchain Queries let your chain
read another chain's state with cryptographic proof

, such as a balance, a pool's reserves or a validator's status. Your logic can then act on remote data without trusting an API. The older asynchronous ICQ application is no longer officially supported in current IBC releases. We integrate or adapt the proof-based approach Neutron runs in production: its interchain-queries module plus an ICQ relayer. The relayer submits key-value data with Merkle proofs, and your chain verifies them against its light client of the counterparty.
IBC middleware: forwarding, rate limits and callbacks
Packet forwarding:
routes a transfer across several chains in one user action.
Rate limiting:

caps how much of an asset can flow through a channel in a time window. This is one of the most effective controls for limiting damage if a connected chain is compromised, and we recommend it for any chain holding meaningful value.
Callbacks:
let modules and contracts react when their packets are acknowledged or time out, which makes multi-step cross-chain workflows reliable.
IBC v2: connecting to Ethereum and EVM networks
IBC v2, also called "IBC Eureka", removes the channel handshake and routes packets directly between light clients. It was built to connect Cosmos chains with
Ethereum and EVM networks

blocks.alt: IBC v2 connection between a Cosmos appchain and Ethereum

c.v: On Ethereum:
IBC Solidity contracts verify your Cosmos chain with a CometBFT light client. Zero-knowledge (SP1) proofs make the signature checks affordable in gas.
On your Cosmos chain:
a light client of Ethereum verifies the other direction.
Where a full light client isn't practical yet:
an attestation client relies on a fixed committee of signers instead. That is a weaker trust assumption, and we say so.
During architecture we show you exactly which trust model each route uses.
Relayer operations

IBC works only while relayers run. Current IBC releases no longer include on-chain relayer fee middleware, so relaying is usually funded by the chain team or a service provider. Budget for it. We cover the following:
Deployment:
Hermes for classic IBC, and the Cosmos Labs relayer for IBC v2 routes where its licence allows.
Configuration:
channel policies and funded relayer wallets.
Monitoring:
alerts on packet backlogs.
Light-client refreshes before expiry:
an expired client freezes the connection until governance intervenes.
IBC vs traditional bridges
Many bridges
secure assets with a multisig or committee. If those keys are stolen or the signers collude, funds can be drained.
IBC
verifies the counterparty chain's consensus on-chain, so its security reduces to the validator sets of the two connected chains.
What it doesn't remove:
if a connected chain is compromised, assets that came from it are exposed. That is why rate limits and careful channel selection still matter.
For other interoperability patterns, see our
cross-chain bridge architecture
guide and our
bridge security engineering
service.

title.v: Smart Contracts on Your Appchain: Native Modules, CosmWasm or Cosmos EVM

c.v: You can run a Cosmos appchain without smart contracts, and many of the best-known chains keep core logic in native modules. A contract environment makes sense when you want third-party developers, faster iteration or an existing contract codebase.
Best for

rows.v: Core protocol logic, per-block automation, privileged operations
Permissioned or open contract platforms, IBC-aware applications
Teams with Solidity code, EVM tooling and EVM users

c.v: Upgrade path

rows.v: Contract migration by an admin, or immutable

c.v: Tooling

rows.v: Rust, CosmWasm libraries, multi-contract test harness

c.v: Interop

rows.v: IBC entry points built in (including IBC v2 in CosmWasm 3)
Precompiles for native modules and ICS-20 transfers

c.v: Watch-outs

rows.v: A bug can halt the chain; fixes need a chain upgrade
Your SDK version is limited by the wasmd release (currently on SDK v0.54)
Pre-1.0 software; gas token must use 18 decimals

c.v: CosmWasm in practice
CosmWasm contracts are written in Rust, compiled to WebAssembly and run inside the chain.
No synchronous calls.
A contract cannot call another directly. It returns messages that execute after it, and it handles their results in a
reply
entry point. This removes the classic reentrancy pattern, but logic errors are still possible, so audits still matter.
Privileged hooks.
A
sudo
entry point lets chain modules or governance call contracts with privileges no user has. This is useful for protocol-controlled contracts.
Upgrades and admin keys.

A contract instantiated with an admin can be migrated to new code. Whether that admin is a multisig, governance, or nobody, which makes the contract immutable, is a security decision we document with you.
Deployment permissions.
Code upload and instantiation can be open to everyone, limited to listed addresses, or gated by governance. Permissioned networks use this to approve each contract before it goes live.
Standards.
Token and NFT contracts follow established CosmWasm specifications (cw20, cw721), so wallets and explorers recognise them.
Cosmos EVM in practice
Cosmos EVM adds an Ethereum-compatible execution layer with Ethereum JSON-RPC, so existing Solidity contracts, MetaMask and EVM tooling work.
Native access.
Precompiled contracts expose native modules, such as staking, distribution, bank and ICS-20 transfers, to Solidity.
Licence and maintenance.
It is open source (Apache-2.0) and maintained by Cosmos Labs.
Version risk.
Its releases are still below 1.0 and some updates are state-breaking. We pin versions and plan upgrades deliberately.
We build contracts in both environments through our
smart contract development
practice. If you are weighing the languages, our
Solidity vs Rust
comparison sets out the trade-offs.

title.v: Staking, Governance and Tokenomics Design

c.v: On a sovereign chain the token is not only a product feature. It is the security budget. We design staking, governance and economics as one system and test them with simulations before genesis.
Staking and slashing parameters
The Cosmos SDK ships with defaults that almost every production chain changes:
a 100-validator active set
a 21-day unbonding period
a 5% slash for double-signing
a 1% slash for downtime
We set each parameter against your threat model:
Unbonding period.
A longer period makes long-range attacks harder and keeps staked capital in place. A shorter one makes staking more attractive.
It also caps the trusting period of the IBC light clients other chains use to track yours. Shorten it, and counterparties must refresh those clients more often.
Slashing and jailing.
Penalties should deter misbehaviour without driving away careful validators over one outage. Double-signing is punished severely, and brief downtime usually less so.
Active set and commission rules.
We decide how many validators earn rewards and set minimum commissions so that validation stays sustainable.
Key rotation.
Cosmos SDK v0.55 lets validators rotate consensus keys without creating a new validator, which helps key hygiene and incident response. CosmWasm chains get it once wasmd supports v0.55.
For reward-distribution patterns beyond staking, see our
staking reward distribution architecture
service.
On-chain governance
The governance module controls parameter changes, treasury spending and software upgrades. We set up these parts:
Deposits
that keep out spam without excluding the community.
Quorum, pass and veto thresholds.
Expedited proposals
for security fixes.
Proposal rights
, meaning who can submit which proposal types.
Consortium chains get governance built around member organisations rather than token-weighted votes. More in our
on-chain governance design
guide.
Token supply, inflation and genesis allocation
Issuance model.
The SDK's default inflation adjusts to keep a target share of tokens staked. Current releases also accept a custom mint function, for fixed schedules, halvings or issuance tied to protocol revenue.
Genesis allocation.
Allocations for the team, investors, community, treasury, ecosystem grants and validator delegation programmes are written into the genesis file. Tokens that unlock over time sit in vesting accounts.
Treasury and community pool.
A share of rewards funds development through governance-controlled spending.
Simulation.
We model staking ratios, yields and dilution under different adoption scenarios before you commit to numbers. You can try the basics with our
token economics simulator
Gas and fee models
Fee tokens.
Accept fees in your native token, a stablecoin, or several approved denominations.
Minimum and dynamic pricing.
Each validator enforces a minimum gas price.
Chains that need congestion pricing can add an EIP-1559-style fee market. Cosmos EVM includes one, and native chains need a maintained implementation.
Sponsored transactions.
The fee-grant module lets your application pay fees for new users, so they can transact before they buy tokens.
Fee routing.
By default, fees go to validators and stakers, with a community-pool share.
A custom fee-routing module can split fees between stakers, a treasury and burns, and governance can adjust the split.
Spam control.
Gas pricing, ante-handler filters and mempool rules protect the chain without blocking legitimate high-volume users.

title.v: Validator and Node Infrastructure

c.v: Your chain is only as reliable as the infrastructure under it. We design and deploy the network layer and prepare your validators to run theirs.

blocks.alt: Cosmos validator infrastructure with sentry nodes, remote signer and monitoring

c.v: Sentry architecture.
Validators sit behind sentry nodes, so the signing node is never exposed to the public peer-to-peer network.
Key management.

Consensus keys live in a remote signer, not on the validator host. Options are the current official Cosmos signer (cosmos-kms) with HSM or cloud-KMS backends, or threshold signing (for example Horcrux) to withstand a single-machine compromise.
Existing networks need to plan their move away from the deprecated TMKMS signer.
Public endpoints.
RPC, gRPC and REST endpoints for wallets, frontends and integrators, with load balancing and rate limits.
Archive nodes for historical queries.
Node bootstrapping.
State-sync and snapshot services let new nodes join quickly instead of replaying the whole chain. Pruning policies keep storage under control.
Monitoring and alerting.
Dashboards and alerts are fed by CometBFT's Prometheus metrics and the SDK's OpenTelemetry support. They cover:
missed blocks
peer count
mempool size
block-time drift
disk growth
relayer backlogs
light-client expiry
Validator onboarding.
For public chains we prepare validator documentation, hardware guidance and the selection criteria for genesis and delegation programmes. Operators are normally chosen on:
operational track record
independent infrastructure
geographic and hosting-provider diversity, so no single cloud region can halt the chain
Our
blockchain monitoring setup guide
explains the monitoring stack in more depth.

title.v: Wallet, Explorer and dApp Integration

c.v: A chain that wallets and explorers can't see is unusable, so we make yours usable from day one:
Wallets:
Cosmos-native wallets such as Keplr and Cosmostation.
MetaMask-compatible wallets for Cosmos EVM chains.
No dependence on a single wallet. Leap, a major Cosmos wallet, shut down in 2026.
Chain registry.
Your chain's endpoints, assets and IBC paths go into the community registry that wallets, explorers and relayers read.
Explorers and indexers.
Users, auditors and your support team need to follow transactions, so we set up both.
Frontend SDKs.
TypeScript clients built on CosmJS and current wallet-connection kits, generated from your protobuf definitions.
Applications.
The dApp, dashboards and admin tools on top of your chain. Our
wallet development
team can build a dedicated wallet if your product needs one.

title.v: Security Engineering and Testing

c.v: A bug in a smart contract can drain that contract. A bug in a chain module can
halt the network or corrupt state for every user
. Our process reflects that difference:
Threat modelling
during architecture. It covers economic attacks, validator collusion, IBC counterparty risk, key compromise and governance capture.
Unit and integration tests
for every message, query and keeper path, including failure cases.
Simulation testing.
The SDK's simulation framework runs large volumes of randomised transactions against the full application.
After each block it checks invariants, such as total supply equalling the sum of balances.
Invariants are enforced in testing, not on the live chain.
Multi-chain end-to-end tests.
Containerised networks run your chain, its counterparties and relayers together. They test transfers, timeouts, ICA flows and upgrades before anything reaches a public network.
Fuzzing
of message handlers and encoding paths.
Determinism and upgrade rehearsal.
We confirm that every node reaches the same state, and we rehearse every upgrade on a copy of real chain state.
Internal security review
, then
independent external audit
of custom modules and contracts before mainnet, with every finding tracked to remediation.
Launch controls:
rate limits on IBC channels
conservative governance thresholds
restricted contract uploads where appropriate
Read more about our
blockchain QA and testing strategy
and our
audit process

title.v: From Testnet to Mainnet: Our Launch Playbook

c.v: Launching a proof-of-stake chain means coordinating independent validators to start the same software from the same state at the same moment. We run it as a rehearsed process:

blocks.alt: Cosmos appchain launch timeline from devnet to mainnet genesis

c.v: Local devnets.
Multi-node networks run continuously in CI.
Internal testnet.
A persistent network on your production configuration, with monitoring, explorer and relayers connected to other test networks.
Public or incentivised testnet.
External validators join, practise operations and earn eligibility for genesis or delegation programmes.
Real usage exposes performance and parameter issues before mainnet.
Security sign-off.
Audit findings are fixed, the upgrade path is rehearsed and launch parameters are frozen.
Genesis ceremony.
We publish the genesis candidate, with balances, vesting and parameters.
Validators submit signed
genesis transactions (gentx)
within a set window.
We assemble and verify the final genesis file and publish its hash.
Launch day.
Validators start their nodes before genesis time, and the chain produces its first block once more than two-thirds of genesis voting power is online.
We stay on a live call with validators until block production, endpoints and IBC are confirmed stable.
Post-launch hardening.
First governance actions, opening IBC channels, starting relayers, and gradually raising the conservative launch limits.
Permissioned chains follow the same process with a smaller, contractually defined validator group, so it is usually shorter.

title.v: After Mainnet: Upgrades, Monitoring and Maintenance

c.v: A Cosmos chain needs active maintenance to stay secure and compatible:

blocks.alt: Cosmos SDK chain upgrade flow using governance and Cosmovisor

c.v: Planned upgrades.
Each change passes a governance proposal that sets an upgrade height.
At that height every node halts. Nodes running Cosmovisor switch to the new binary automatically, and an upgrade handler migrates the stored state.
We write and rehearse the handlers and coordinate validators.
Supported releases.
Cosmos Labs supports at most two release lines of the SDK, CometBFT and Cosmos EVM at a time, and older lines stop receiving security patches.
We plan your upgrade calendar so the chain never runs unsupported software.
Security patching.

title.v: Frequently Asked Questions

c.v: What is Cosmos SDK appchain development?

It is the process of building an application-specific blockchain with the Cosmos SDK: a dedicated chain whose rules, fees, governance and validator set are designed around one product. The work covers custom Go modules, consensus configuration, token economics, IBC connections, testing, and launching and operating the network.
When should a business build its own appchain instead of deploying smart contracts?

When the product needs control a contract can't provide. Examples include custom transaction ordering, protocol-level automation, its own fee model, permissioning, or independence from another chain's congestion and governance. If the main need is fast launch and access to an existing ecosystem's users and liquidity, smart contracts are usually the better start.
What is the difference between the Cosmos SDK, CometBFT and the Cosmos Hub?

The Cosmos SDK is the Go framework for the chain's application logic. CometBFT is the consensus engine that orders transactions and finalises blocks. The Cosmos Hub is one independent chain built with these tools. Your appchain does not need its permission, token or security.
How is the Cosmos SDK different from Substrate (Polkadot SDK)?

The Cosmos SDK uses Go. Each chain usually secures itself with its own validators, interoperates through IBC, and upgrades by swapping the node binary at a governance-approved height. Substrate uses Rust with a WebAssembly runtime, typically takes security from the Polkadot relay chain, uses XCM, and supports forkless runtime upgrades. See our
Polkadot and Substrate development
page for that path.
Which Cosmos SDK and CometBFT versions will you build on?

We use a currently supported release family and choose the exact version based on your execution environment. For example, CosmWasm chains are limited by the latest wasmd release. We avoid retracted releases and plan your first upgrade before the chosen line reaches end of life.
Do we need our own validators, and can you provide or run nodes?

A public proof-of-stake chain needs independent validators, and recruiting them is part of the launch plan. A permissioned chain uses a known group of organisations under proof of authority. We can deploy and operate the non-validator infrastructure (RPC, archive, relayer and monitoring nodes). We also prepare documentation and onboarding for the validators who will secure the network.
How are validators selected for a new Cosmos chain?

Usually through a public or incentivised testnet, where operators prove their reliability and then submit genesis transactions. Common criteria are testnet uptime, security practices, independent infrastructure, and geographic and hosting-provider diversity. Many projects also run delegation programmes to spread stake across the set.
What is IBC and how is it different from a bridge?

IBC is a protocol for sending tokens and data between blockchains. Each chain runs an on-chain light client of the other, so messages are verified cryptographically rather than approved by a separate committee. Relayers only deliver messages. Many traditional bridges depend on a multisig or external validator group, which is an extra trust assumption.
Can a Cosmos appchain connect to Ethereum?

Yes. IBC v2 connects Cosmos chains to Ethereum and EVM networks through IBC Solidity contracts and light clients. Some routes use attestation committees, and we set out the trust model of each route during architecture. If you need Ethereum tooling and wallets on your chain itself, Cosmos EVM adds Solidity and MetaMask compatibility.
Should we use CosmWasm, Cosmos EVM or native modules?

Native modules suit core, performance-critical protocol logic. CosmWasm suits an IBC-aware Rust contract platform, especially a permissioned one. Cosmos EVM suits teams whose code or users are already in the Ethereum ecosystem. Many chains combine native modules with one contract environment.
Can smart contracts be upgraded after launch, and who controls that?

In CosmWasm, a contract with an admin can be migrated to new code, and the admin can be a multisig, governance or no one at all. In Cosmos EVM, upgrades use proxy patterns. Native modules change only through a governance-approved chain upgrade. We agree the control model with you before deployment.
How much does it cost to build a Cosmos appchain?

It depends on the number and complexity of custom modules, any smart contract layer, the number of IBC connections, the security model, audit scope and post-launch support. We provide a scoped estimate after a short discovery phase. Also budget for ongoing validator incentives, infrastructure and relaying.
How long does Cosmos SDK development take?

A focused permissioned chain can reach production in a few months. A public proof-of-stake appchain with custom economics, contracts and several IBC connections usually takes six months or more, including audits and a public testnet.
What happens if the chain halts?

Validators coordinate to fix the cause, usually through a patched binary and an agreed restart. That is why incident runbooks, validator communication channels and rehearsed emergency upgrades are part of our launch work, not an afterthought.
Can the chain be private or permissioned?

Yes. Cosmos SDK chains can restrict validators to approved organisations, gate contract uploads behind governance, limit which accounts transact, and keep endpoints private. Some ready-made enterprise modules carry commercial licence terms, which we review during architecture.
Can you migrate our existing dApp to its own Cosmos chain?
Yes. We map your contracts and state to native modules, CosmWasm or Cosmos EVM. We then plan token and state migration, IBC or bridge routes for existing users, and a cut-over that keeps funds safe.
Can you work alongside our in-house engineering team?

Yes. We can own the full build, or we can embed with your Go or Rust developers to handle architecture, specialist modules, IBC, security or launch. Full documentation and handover are standard either way.
